articles.title: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis
articles.summary: More than 50 protests took place on Saturday after the government failed to get emergency legislation through parliament.
articles.body:
Major protest in Spain as millions struggle to find an affordable home

Tens of thousands of people have protested across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to pass emergency housing legislation.

About 50 marches took place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona.

"There is a lot of anger in the streets," a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union said. Clashes have taken place between some protesters and police in the city.

The measures put forward by Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase.

Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property.

Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.

His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament.

Photographs showed protesters in the east coast city of Valencia clashing with police officers on Saturday near arts centre Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía, which was hosting a real estate summit.

Several protesters removed barriers and threw objects at officers, who responded with rubber bullets, Spanish media reported. Public broadcaster RTVE said nine police officers were injured and five people were arrested.

One of the biggest demonstration happened in the capital, Madrid, where estimates of the number of participants varied widely. The city's Tenants' Union said there were 500,000, while officials put the figure at 70,000.

Demonstrators held banners reading "There won't be peace for rentism" and "I study to have a future, not to have a tiny apartment". They shook the keys they were holding and chanted: "We have the keys of all the city".

Some had also camped in one of the city's main squares, Puerta del Sol, for days.

One protester, David, told RTVE ahead of the protest: "We're not here for pleasure or comfort. We're here out of conviction."

Another protester, 26-year-old librarian Marcos Sainz, told AFP news agency that he used to share a two-bedroom flat with friends, paying 900 euros (£766) a month in rent. Today, he said a one-bedroom flat often costs 1,000 euros.

Sainz said he would protest against rent rises "until someone dares to regulate it all", or "we'll all have to leave Madrid".

Spanish police said they had arrested three members of a far-right group, some of whom had performed Nazi salutes, as they tried to reach demonstrators in the square.

On Friday night, Madrid's Tenants' Union said that although the government's proposed measures were insufficient, the rejection of the proposed legislation "exacerbates the housing crisis which is costing the working class their lives".

It is calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.

The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two decrees.

The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by so-called "vulture funds".

The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenants' Union.

MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.

Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.

However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.

Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September.

The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued.

The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.

House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE.

The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents.

It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.80 per square metre and €22.70 per square metre respectively.

articles.title: In 2023, a London house-clearance crew found two old computers buried under boxes; they were two of only three known surviving Q1 microcomputers, and the 1972 model later sold for £37,179
articles.summary: Discover the rare Q1 microcomputers, one of only three surviving models, found during a house clearance in London and sold for astounding prices at auction.
articles.body: The world's first fully integrated desktop computer was found among boxes during a London house clearance in 2023, with one of the rare machines later sold for £37,179 at auction. The computers were discovered by house-clearance firm Just Clear while workers were clearing a London property. The find included a 1972 Q1 desktop microcomputer with an internal printer and its slightly later sibling, the Q1 Lite.Only three Q1 microcomputers are known to have survived, making the two machines particularly rare. A companion printer designed for the Q1 Lite was also found during the clearance. The three devices were later offered for the first time at auction by Dallas-based Heritage Auctions. The 1972 Q1 achieved the highest price, selling for £37,179. The Q1 Lite sold for £8,316, while its companion printer fetched £1,175.All three machines were sold without a reserve.Computers that predated the Apple 1The Q1 dates back to 1972, four years before Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs introduced the Apple 1.The machine used a microprocessor-based architecture that allowed it to deliver capabilities that had previously been associated with much larger computer systems.Valarie Spiegel, Heritage Auctions' director of video games, said the technology allowed the Q1 to “punch well above its weight” and established an important precedent for the computing industry.The Q1 was also far from affordable by the standards of the time. The machines would have cost the equivalent of more than £70,000 each, making them too expensive to be marketed for individual use.Despite that limitation, the Q1 represented an early step towards the development of computers that could eventually become part of everyday life.Rare machines went on public displayThe computers did not go directly from the London house clearance to the auction block.The Q1, Q1 Lite and companion printer were displayed at Kingston University in London in February 2024, as part of an exhibition titled Creating the Everything Device: Showcasing the Machines That Built the Future.The exhibition focused on early computers and gaming machines and placed the newly discovered Q1s alongside other examples of early technology.Paul Neve, a senior lecturer at Kingston University, said having two Q1 machines available for the exhibition offered an opportunity to show the technology that preceded modern computers.“It is a real bonus being able to feature two Q1s, the world’s earliest microcomputers, at Kingston University,” Neve told New Atlas.He said the computers developed during the 1970s and 1980s helped establish the foundations for modern machines used for work, communication, productivity and entertainment.First auction made value uncertainThe Heritage sale was also significant because the machines had never previously been auctioned.Before the bidding began, Sara Balbi, managing director of Heritage Auctions' London office, said there was no established auction record for the Q1s that could indicate how much buyers might pay.“Keep in mind these have never been to auction, and there is no record or precedent set for them. We'll have to see what the market decides,” Balbi said.The eventual results put a value on the rare pieces of computing history.The 1972 Q1 with its internal printer sold for £37,179, while the later Q1 Lite reached £8,316. articles.title: India's political will needed to extradite Sheikh Hasina: Bangladesh
articles.summary: DHAKA: Bangladesh on Sunday hoped India would act on its request for former PM Sheikh Hasina's extradition and expedite the process, saying that \"while
articles.body: DHAKA: Bangladesh on Sunday hoped India would act on its request for former PM Sheikh Hasina's extradition and expedite the process, saying that "while legal process is certainly a factor, political will is also essential".The remarks came a day after Indian high commissioner to Dhaka Dinesh Trivedi at the Bay of Bengal Conversation made it clear the legal process concerning extradition is ongoing and no time-frame can be given as courts are involved. He had said that "again and again, Indian govt has replied to this that there is a process, and the process is legal, and it is well structured. So, as far as that is concerned, the process is on"."While the legal process is certainly a factor, political will is also essential. We hope govt of India will focus on expediting the ongoing extradition process to bring the accused back. Both countries must possess political will. We certainly have political will, and they (India) need to have it as well," state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam told reporterswhen asked about Trivedi's remarks.Meanwhile, outgoing Bangladesh high commissioner to India Md Riaz Hamidullah Sunday met Indian external affairs minister Dr S Jaishankar in New Delhi and discussed issues of mutual interest.During his 18-month stint in India as high commissioner, Riaz said he tried to quietly advance Bangladesh-India relations, premised on mutual trust, dignity and shared benefits.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tarcísio terá 65 dos 94 deputados da Alesp em sua base de apoio | G1
articles.standfirst: Bloco formado por dez partidos terá mais de dois terços das cadeiras da Assembleia Legislativa a partir de 2027. Oposição será liderada por PT e PSOL.
articles.summary: Bloco formado por dez partidos terá mais de dois terços das cadeiras da Assembleia Legislativa a partir de 2027. Oposição será liderada por PT e PSOL.
articles.body:
Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos) discursa pela primeira vez na Alesp como novo governador de SP neste 1 de janeiro de 2023. — Foto: Divulgação/GESP

Os partidos que integraram a coalizão responsável pela reeleição do governador Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos) conquistaram 65 das 94 cadeiras da Assembleia Legislativa de São Paulo (Alesp) nas eleições deste domingo (4). O resultado garante ao governador uma ampla maioria para o segundo mandato e reforça a predominância do campo de centro e direita no Legislativo paulista.

O bloco governista é formado por PL, Republicanos, PSD, MDB, PP, Podemos, União Brasil, Novo, PRD e PSDB. Juntas, as siglas elegeram mais de dois terços da Assembleia, superando com folga os 48 votos necessários para aprovar projetos de lei ordinários e também os 57 votos para aprovar mudanças na Constituição do estado.

Além do PL, também tiveram papel relevante na vitória governista o PSD, com nove deputados eleitos, o Republicanos e o Podemos, com seis cadeiras cada, além de MDB e PP, que conquistaram cinco vagas cada. O União Brasil elegeu quatro parlamentares.

A oposição, por sua vez, seguirá liderada pelo PT, que elegeu 16 deputados estaduais. Apesar de manter a condição de segunda maior bancada da Casa, o partido terá um parlamentar a menos do que atualmente. A legenda foi puxada pela votação de Eduardo Suplicy, segundo candidato mais votado do estado, com 654.627 votos.

Eduarda Campopiano (PL) e Eduardo Suplicy (PT) são os deputados estaduais mais votados de São Paulo — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram e Will Shutter/Câmara dos Deputados

O PSOL foi o principal destaque da oposição. A sigla saltou de cinco para nove deputados estaduais e passará a dividir com o PSD a condição de terceira maior bancada da Assembleia. Entre os eleitos estão Sofia Favero, terceira candidata mais votada da eleição, Carlos Giannazi e Paula da Bancada Feminista.

A composição da próxima legislatura indica que Tarcísio de Freitas chegará ao segundo mandato em situação mais confortável do que a encontrada no início de sua primeira gestão. Ao longo dos últimos quatro anos, o governador conseguiu aprovar projetos considerados estratégicos, como a privatização da Sabesp, graças a uma base ampla no Legislativo.

Os 20 deputados estaduais mais votados de São Paulo em 2026

Paula da Bancada Feminista (PSOL) – 326.190 votos

Monica das Pretas (PSOL) – 159.100 votos

Bruna Furlan (Republicanos) – 157.381 votos

articles.title: FBI arrests woman accused of surveilling Taiwanese president's son for China
articles.summary: Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was arrested on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.
articles.body:
The FBI arrested a suspected Chinese agent at Los Angeles International Airport after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's U.S.-based son, law enforcement sources told CBS News.

Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was cuffed by federal law enforcement on Sunday before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China, from LAX, on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.

Zhang's husband Edric Ding, a realtor at the same firm, told CBS News when reached by phone Sunday: "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.

It was not immediately clear if Zhang has an attorney.

A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of traveling to Seattle, Washington, in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.

Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.

Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.

"If the PRC [People's Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC," wrote FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the Oct. 3, 2026, criminal complaint.

Taiwan has been the focus of high geopolitical tensions for decades . It asserts its independence, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. The island is in a key position astride major shipping lanes, and is where many of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are manufactured.

CBS News reached out to the Taiwanese consulate for comment.

The complaint said Zhang, 34, and a man named only as "Individual 1" flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to their target's home.

Images from a neighbor's security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two "appearing to film" Ting-Yu, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening.

CBS News matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu.

Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler: "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint.

The FBI agent wrote that the texts from the Chinese messaging app WeChat were obtained from a search warrant on Zhang's iCloud account.

"Zhang was in contact with at least two people whom she appeared to acknowledge worked for the PRC government," the agent wrote.

The complaint claims Zhang was introduced in June 2025 to one of the Chinese government officials by a classmate from her alma mater, Beijing's University of International Relations, which Holt said has close ties to the Ministry of State Security.

Holt's affidavit claims Zhang booked a private room in Changsha, China, during a June 2025 trip, where she allegedly met the government official and received her surveillance mission.

She later texted the official, "I can take care of this thing," according to the complaint.

On Aug. 26, 2025, Zhang wrote: "I will be busy with work in L.A. this week. I will probably go to Seattle next week," and the official replied: "Ok. Thank you for your hard work," the complaint said.

Zhang is a licensed California realtor with JC Pacific Capital Inc. Her Zillow profile says she has 130 sales and listings around Los Angeles and neighboring counties.

Ting-Yu received his bachelor's in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, in 2012; a master's in Bioengineering Innovation and Design from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, the following year; then a PhD from the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Washington, according to a profile from one of his academic publications.

Taiwan TV news station SETN reported that he met his Taiwanese wife while studying for his doctorate. They married in 2018 and had a child in the U.S. in 2020, according to CNA , Taiwan's national news agency.

Chinese government agents have previously been caught spying on and harassing Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists in the U.S.

Federal prosecutors said Shujun Wang , 75, infiltrated and informed on a Chinese pro-democracy group in Queens, New York, for the Chinese Ministry of State Security for 17 years. He was convicted in 2024 of acting as a foreign agent.

Two people were arrested in April 2023 for their involvement in an unofficial Chinese police station in Manhattan set up to monitor Chinese dissidents.

The Justice Department has warned of a plan by the Chinese security services called Operation Fox Hunt aimed at repatriating wanted Chinese nationals around the world, which targets enemies of the regime.

New York-based Quanzhong An, who prosecutors say is a leader of the U.S. wing of Operation Fox Hunt, was sentenced in March 2025 after harassing a Chinese dissident in an attempt to bring them back to China.

In California, former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged with acting as a Chinese agent in May. She admitted to being paid to spread pro-Chinese government propaganda in the U.S., including an essay on her blog denying "forced labor" in China.

articles.title: US pulls all bombers from key UK base after suspected Iran-linked terror plot
articles.summary: The Pentagon says its bomber force remains ready for global strikes after aircraft deployed to RAF Fairford returned to the United States.
articles.body: All U.S. Air Force bombers in the U.K. were returned to their home bases in the United States following a suspected terror plot that U.S. officials have suggested may be linked to Iran targeting a U.S. military facility last week, officials said. About a dozen B-1 bombers were among the aircraft removed from Royal Air Force (RAF) Station Fairford in Gloucestershire, England, a U.S. official told Fox News. The base is the only European forward operating location for American heavy bombers. "We can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States," a department official said. The Pentagon emphasized that despite the relocation, the bomber fleet remains fully prepared to launch long-range strike missions directly from the continental United States whenever needed. FOILED TERROR PLOT AT BOMBER BASE SIGNALS WIDER THREAT TO US MILITARY INSTALLATIONS: EXPERT "The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime," the official said. RAF Fairford functions as a key European base for heavy American strategic bombers has supported U.S. military operations, including missions targeting Iranian sites. IRAN COULD MOVE SHADOW WAR IN A DANGEROUS DIRECTION, EXPERTS WARN ON BACK OF TWO POSSIBLE TERROR ATTACKS Last Sunday, U.K. officials said three suspicious vehicles containing fuel accelerants were found near RAF Fairford. "We can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found. However, a quantity of petrol was recovered," officials said. Authorities began investigating potential ties to Iranian state proxies and eventually arrested a British-Iranian dual national "on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts." Secretary of State Marco Rubio later said the suspected plot "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor." President Donald Trump last week also told reporters that the incident may have been connected to Iran, which the United States has been at war with since February. Police, however, said all the suspects have been released on bail, adding that the investigation remains ongoing. articles.title: California realtor nabbed at LAX in alleged China spy case targeting Taiwan president’s relative
articles.summary: FBI agents caught Wanying Zhang at LAX before she boarded a flight to China, accused of secretly surveilling a relative of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.
articles.body: A California realtor accused of spying on a Taiwanese official’s family for Beijing was arrested at LAX as she tried to leave for China, federal authorities announced Sunday. Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine, also known as "Heather," allegedly worked with an associate to photograph and record the family outside their Seattle-area home, according to a criminal complaint obtained by Fox News Digital. "We just arrested a Chinese foreign agent at LAX attempting to depart for China," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli wrote on X. CHINESE SPY INFILTRATION: MAYOR’S BUST ADDS TO GROWING TIMELINE OF FOREIGN INFLUENCE CREEPING INTO US Essayli said FBI Los Angeles agents arrested Zhang on a federal charge of acting as an unregistered agent of the People’s Republic of China. She allegedly traveled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and sent them photos, videos and license plate information. FEDS SAY US CITIZEN GATHERED INFORMATION ON AMERICAN TARGETS FOR CHINESE COMMUNIST PARTY "She coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection," Essayli wrote. "She never notified the Attorney General she was acting for a foreign government, a federal offense." Speaking on "The Big Weekend Show" Sunday, Essayli said Zhang is a naturalized U.S. citizen and confirmed the alleged surveillance targeted a relative of Taiwan’s president. "She was conducting surveillance on behalf of the Chinese government. She was acting as a foreign agent," Essayli said. "And she was spying on a relative of the president of Taiwan here in the U.S." He said agents arrested her as she tried to board a flight to Shanghai. FBI Director Kash Patel also issued a warning to foreign adversaries following Zhang’s arrest. "Foreign adversaries take note: America is no longer a safe place to run your espionage operations," Patel said. "Allegedly surveil a foreign leader’s family on U.S. soil for the PRC — and try to catch a flight back to Shanghai? Not happening." "This FBI is hunting threats to our national security wherever they hide — and bringing them to justice," he added. The alleged target was Ting-Yu Lai, the U.S.-based son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, CBS News reported, citing law enforcement sources. The complaint does not name him. "Saw him. Young male. It’s that young one," Zhang allegedly messaged a Chinese government contact while outside the home. "I am videorecording," she allegedly added before sending two license plate numbers. CHINESE NATIONAL ARRESTED AT JFK AFTER ALLEGEDLY PHOTOGRAPHING US MILITARY AIRCRAFT AT NEBRASKA BASE Zhang and her associate allegedly flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and waited near the family’s home. When the target returned, a neighbor’s security camera captured the pair quickly sitting up and holding out what appeared to be phones to photograph or record the family, according to the affidavit. Family members, including children, arrived shortly afterward. "While individual 1 took pictures, Zhang reclined her seat as if to avoid being seen," FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt wrote. Days later, Zhang allegedly told her associate to transfer the surveillance photos through AirDrop. BRONX MAN CONVICTED OF RUNNING SECRET CHINESE POLICE STATION IN MANHATTAN USED TO MONITOR DISSIDENTS "Seattle pictures, don’t send via WeChat or text. Must be sent over the air. I have to send it back. He wants me to send it back today," she said in an audio message described in the affidavit. Holt said he believed the instruction was intended to help avoid detection. The associate later told Zhang he had deleted the photos and cleared them from his deleted folder, which Holt described as an apparent attempt to destroy evidence. CHINA’S INFLUENCE MACHINE: FEDERAL RECORDS EXPOSE BEIJING’S PUSH TO SWAY AMERICA Investigators believe Zhang received the surveillance assignment during a June 2025 meeting with a Chinese government contact in Changsha, China. "I can take care of this thing," she allegedly told the contact. DEMS UNDER FIRE FOR ‘MALIGN CHINESE INFLUENCE’ AS SHOCKING SPY MAYOR DONATIONS UNCOVERED: ‘HOW MANY MORE?’ Holt warned that information about a senior Taiwanese official’s relatives, including their homes and cars, could give Beijing leverage over Taiwan’s president during a potential conflict. "Engaging in surveillance of a close relative of a high-ranking member of Taiwan’s government is not normal diplomatic behavior, especially inside of the United States," he wrote. Essayli warned on "The Big Weekend Show" that the threat extends beyond California. "China’s very good at using people who are already here," he said. "I don’t think it’s unique to California. It is happening nationwide." Essayli said Zhang is scheduled to appear Monday in federal court in Los Angeles and noted that defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty. The arrest comes months after former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged in a separate case with acting as an agent of China involving paid efforts to spread pro-Beijing propaganda in the United States. articles.title: Attorney for accused Cornell student calls on Letitia James to step aside over prior comments
articles.summary: New York Attorney General Letitia James faces a recusal call after her prior public statements appeared to support the accuser in the Cornell alleged sexual assault case.
articles.body: New York Attorney General Letitia James is facing a call to step aside from the investigation into the alleged Cornell sexual assault after an attorney for one of the accused students questioned whether she had publicly accepted the allegations before taking over the case. Andrew Miltenberg, who represents one of seven former fraternity members accused in a civil lawsuit, said James’ earlier statements supporting the accuser created an "avoidable question about the appearance of impartiality." "The concern is whether the public can have confidence that the investigation begins without any predetermined view of the facts," Miltenberg said in a statement to Fox News. AOC'S DRAMATIC RETELLING OF CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS COLLIDES WITH COMPLAINT DETAILS Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed the attorney general’s office as special prosecutor Thursday, replacing Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten in the investigation into an alleged October 2024 sexual assault at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house. The woman, identified in court papers as Jane Doe, alleges seven former fraternity members drugged and sexually assaulted her. The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated. No criminal charges have been filed against the seven men. DELETED EMAIL DETAILS ALLEGED TRUMP-TARGETING PUSH INSIDE LETITIA JAMES’ OFFICE: ‘FIND AND PURSUE CRIMES’ Miltenberg’s objection centers on comments James made before her office was appointed to lead the criminal investigation. She publicly described what the woman had "been forced to endure" as "horrific and unacceptable" and told her, together with "all survivors," that "we stand with you." When asked at Friday’s news conference about her objectivity in light of the Facebook post, James said, "I will not comment on a Facebook post." Criminal defense attorney and Fox News contributor Donna Rotunno also questioned James’ role during an appearance on Fox News’ "The Big Weekend Show." "But it should be fair. It should be impartial. And it should not be from someone who’s already made a public statement on Facebook about it," Rotunno said of reopening the investigation. James has said the investigation will be guided by "the facts and the law." Miltenberg said his concerns were not political and did not diminish the seriousness of sexual assault allegations. TRUMP LAWYERS TARGET WHAT LETITIA JAMES WON’T SAY ABOUT EVIDENCE IN $450M CASE "There is nothing improper about expressing compassion for someone who reports a sexual assault," he said. "But there is an important difference between supporting a person who makes an allegation and appearing to accept the factual premise of that allegation before conducting an investigation." He urged James to personally recuse herself while allowing senior prosecutors in her office who have not publicly commented on the merits of the allegations to handle the investigation. "That would not weaken the investigation. It would strengthen it," Miltenberg said. He argued that the same concerns about independence and public confidence that prompted the appointment of a special prosecutor should apply to the person leading the replacement investigation. LETITIA JAMES’ RE-ELECTION CUSHION SHRINKS AS LITTLE-KNOWN CHALLENGER STARTS TURNING HEADS "I am not suggesting that Attorney General James does not believe she can be fair," he said. The case drew renewed scrutiny after Doe filed a civil lawsuit Sept. 16, nearly two years after the alleged assault. The complaint also names Cornell, fraternity entities, Doe’s sorority and a local bar, among others, alleging failures to protect her. BIDEN-APPOINTED JUDGE HANDS LETITIA JAMES SETBACK IN LATEST TRUMP LEGAL CLASH Van Houten initially declined to pursue criminal charges, saying the signed statement his office received from Cornell University Police did not establish a crime under New York law. He said prosecutors assumed Doe’s account was true and that her credibility was "never in question." He later reopened the investigation after the lawsuit surfaced. CORNELL PRESIDENT SAYS UNIVERSITY 'MUST DO BETTER' ON HANDLING OF SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS Questions about the original investigation intensified when CBS News presented Van Houten with a fuller transcript of Doe’s police interviews that he said his office had never received. "That wasn’t information that I had," Van Houten said, adding that its existence "changes the landscape for me." Rotunno also questioned why prosecutors had not sought the complete investigative record before deciding against charges. "The real question is, why didn’t the DA ask for every piece of information that the campus police gathered?" she said on "The Big Weekend Show." She warned against allowing public reaction to drive the case. "We are watching the court of public opinion take over here when we don’t know the facts," Rotunno said. Cornell has separately agreed to an independent review of its handling of the allegations. University President Michael Kotlikoff said its disciplinary process resulted in two expulsions and two suspensions of at least two semesters. One student graduated before discipline could be imposed, and two were found not responsible for sexual misconduct. Those proceedings are separate from the criminal investigation. Cornell previously told Fox News it "fully support[s] the appointment of a special prosecutor" and is committed to "an independent external review of all aspects of how Cornell has handled this case." Miltenberg said any decision about criminal charges should come from prosecutors whose impartiality the public can trust. Fox News' Michelle Langer and Michael Dorgan contributed to this report.

articles.title: All-out war in Yemen: Saudi-backed govt launches military drive to retake Houthi-held territory
articles.summary: Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi on Sunday announced the launch of military operations to retake territory held by the Iran-backed Houthis, declaring that
articles.body: Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi on Sunday announced the launch of military operations to retake territory held by the Iran-backed Houthis, declaring that government forces would seek to restore state authority across the country.“Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory,” Al-Alimi said in a televised address, according to the BBC.The announcement followed a major Houthi offensive last month, during which the Iran-backed group seized territory along Yemen's Red Sea coastline, including areas around the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait. The Houthis have also continued to advance around Taiz, a key government-held city in southwestern Yemen.The escalation has also brought Saudi Arabia directly into the latest phase of the conflict. The Houthis claimed they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area, saying the attacks were carried out in response to 50 Saudi-led coalition strikes in Yemen over 12 hours.“Both operations successfully achieved their objectives,” Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said, according to the BBC.The immediate battlefield focus is Taiz, where the Houthis have reportedly cut a vital supply route linking the city with Aden, the interim capital of the Yemeni government.AFP, citing three Yemeni military sources, reported that the move has effectively left Taiz surrounded.“They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it,” Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House, told AFP.Government and Saudi-led coalition forces have been targeting Houthi military positions as the government seeks to weaken the group before attempting to reclaim territory.The latest escalation comes against the backdrop of Yemen's war, which began in 2014 when the Houthis seized Sanaa and expanded their control across northern Yemen. Saudi Arabia intervened the following year at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognised government.The Houthis' latest offensive has now altered the battlefield, giving them greater control of Yemen's Red Sea coastline and increasing their leverage over the Bab al-Mandab shipping route.The developments also pose a direct risk to Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure. articles.title: Apple is making changes to its OS for Macs after users' complain about Meta's AI Agent Muse accessing their 'private data'
articles.summary: Apple is planning to change its Mac operating system, and the reason are AI Agents.
articles.body: Apple is planning to change its Mac operating system, and the reason are AI Agents. The company wants to make it more clear to users when AI agents ask ​to access all of the data on their Macs. The announcement comes after some users have criticized Meta's ‌Muse, an AI agent for accessing their private messages. While on ​Apple's iPhones and iPads, no single app can access data inside another ​app by default, company's Macs are ⁠more flexible. Apple Macs come with a 'Full Disk Access' option that allows apps such as cloud ​backup services to access all the data on a machine, with a user's permission.In an update posted on its developer website, Apple said that some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk. "Going forward, we will introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely ​wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so ​with very explicit user action," Apple wrote."As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, ‌the ⁠risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy."Apple's announcement comes after a technology ​columnist in Inc magazine accused ​Meta's Muse of ⁠reading private messages on his Mac. "In fact, I remember explicitly choosing not to let it have access to my messages, calendar, and other personal information," he wrote. He claimed that he had not enabled Full Disk Access and further added that when he asked Muse to explain how this occurred, the AI said that it was syncing his "device notifications." Similarly, a YouTuber named Matt Robb recently said that Muse mishandled a task in which he was selling things on Facebook Marketplace, leading to his address being shared.Meta spokesperson Andy Stone disputed the claims saying that Muse's access to Apple's Messages app ​is strictly ⁠opt-in. "You have to enable both Full Disk Access and the Messages connector for Muse to be able to read your Messages content," Stone wrote on social media platform X, opens new tab. "It ⁠can't read ​your Messages unless you do this. And it ​can be revoked at any time."Apple's complete statement on updates to Full Disk Access in macOS"We give developers powerful APIs to build incredible capabilities into their apps for Apple products, backed by a set of controls designed to protect users’ private data. Full Disk Access largely sidesteps these controls in order to allow backup apps to function properly on the Mac. Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems -- including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history -- without users’ full knowledge and understanding. For communication apps, this can also compromise the privacy of the people users are communicating with.""Going forward, we will introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action. Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy."You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2013, an American billionaire backed $260 million to transform New York’s damaged Pier 54, creating Little Island eight years later
articles.summary: Little Island rises from the Hudson River where an ageing New York pier once stood, its planted slopes resting on a series of concrete structures that
articles.body: Little Island rises from the Hudson River where an ageing New York pier once stood, its planted slopes resting on a series of concrete structures that make the park appear to float above the water. The 2.4-acre public space opened in May 2021 after years of planning, legal disputes and construction, as reported by The New York Times. It was largely funded by billionaire media executive Barry Diller through the Diller-von Furstenberg Family Foundation, turning the former Pier 54 site into a new part of Hudson River Park. What began as a proposal to repair a damaged pier has since become a heavily visited waterfront destination. Reportedly, by 2026, Little Island had welcomed more than 7.5 million visitors.How Little Island gave New York’s Pier 54 a new purposeThe site has a long history before Little Island appeared. Pier 54 was where survivors of the Titanic arrived in New York in 1912 aboard the RMS Carpathia. Three years later, the RMS Lusitania departed from the same pier before being sunk by a German U-boat off Ireland, as reported by The New York Times.The structure later became part of the city's waterfront recreation scene. It hosted summer events and concerts and, from the 1980s, became associated with New York's LGBTQ community and the annual Dance on the Pier event. By the time Hurricane Sandy damaged the pier in 2012, however, its condition had become a growing problem, as reported by Hudson River Park and Little Island.In 2013, Diller and the Hudson River Park Trust began looking at ways to repair and reactivate the site. Rather than simply restoring the old structure, the proposal developed into something much more unusual: a new public park built over the river.Barry Diller backed a $260 million transformationReuters reported Diller's contribution ultimately became the financial foundation of the project. Contemporary reports put the project at about $260 million, with the Diller-von Furstenberg Family Foundation providing the principal private funding. Hudson River Park's own financial records later put the completed project cost at approximately $250 million, including $21.2 million funded by the Trust.Reportedly, the foundation also committed to paying for Little Island's maintenance for its first 20 years. That arrangement meant the park could operate as part of the wider public waterfront without leaving all of its above-deck operating costs with the Hudson River Park Trust.Diller brought in British designer Thomas Heatherwick, whose studio developed the distinctive concept. Landscape architect Signe Nielsen and her team at Mathews Nielsen Landscape Architects were responsible for the planting and outdoor environment, while engineering firm Arup worked on the complex structural system.The result was not a conventional pier. It was a park assembled from 132 tulip-shaped concrete pots supported by piles driven into the riverbed. Construction company Kiewit says 267 cylindrical piles were installed to support the structures, with the concrete pots varying in height from 10 to 30 feet.How 350 plant species transformed Little Island above the Hudson RiverFrom the shoreline, the unusual engineering is difficult to miss. The concrete supports rise from the water like a cluster of oversized flower stems, carrying a landscape that slopes, bends and changes elevation across the small site.More than 350 species of flowers, trees and shrubs were incorporated into the park. Paths wind between lawns and planted areas, while the elevated position gives visitors views across the Hudson and towards Manhattan.There are performance spaces within the landscape rather than a single conventional building. The largest is a 687-seat amphitheatre facing the river. A smaller stage and lawn provide another setting for performances and community events. The park was designed to combine everyday public use with arts programming, rather than functioning simply as a viewpoint or garden.That mix has remained central to the site's operation. Little Island's programme has included performances, workshops, educational activities and community events, alongside the ordinary business of people walking, sitting on the grass or looking out across the water.The project almost disappeared before it openedLittle Island was not built without opposition. The proposal became entangled in years of legal disputes, with opponents challenging aspects of the plan and its relationship with the wider Hudson River Park.The New York Times reported, at one stage, after the litigation appeared unlikely to end, Diller withdrew his support. A subsequent agreement brokered by then-Governor Andrew Cuomo helped put the project back on track. The settlement also included commitments involving wildlife habitat and improvements elsewhere in Hudson River Park.The dispute meant that a project initially conceived years earlier took a long route to completion. Little Island eventually opened to the public on May 21, 2021, after the pandemic had already delayed the planned opening period.Millions of visitors have since crossed onto Little IslandThe scale of its use changed quickly. Little Island says it received more than 1 million visitors during its first year. By July 2024, the organisation reported 4.6 million visitors since opening. That figure has continued to rise. Little Island's current information says the park has welcomed more than 7.5 million visitors since opening in 2021. That puts the small waterfront park firmly into the millions-of-visitors category despite its limited physical size.The wider Hudson River Park also attracts substantial footfall. The four-mile waterfront park stretches from Chambers Street to West 59th Street and records more than 17 million visits each year, according to the Hudson River Park Trust. Little Island forms just one part of that larger public landscape.Its popularity has also required practical controls. During its opening period, timed entry was introduced during busier hours to manage crowds, particularly while pandemic restrictions were still affecting public spaces.You use AI every day. articles.body: The US military killed four people in a strike on a suspected drug-trafficking vessel in the Caribbean Sea, the US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said on Sunday. The operation is the latest in a series of attacks by Washington on vessels it claims are involved in narcotics trafficking, drawing criticism from human rights organisations and international experts over their legality.In a statement posted on X, SOUTHCOM said Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere conducted a "lethal, kinetic strike" on a high-speed vessel operating along established drug-trafficking routes in the Caribbean."Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking," the command said, describing those killed in the operation as "narco-terrorists."SOUTHCOM also released footage of the operation showing the vessel moving through the water before being struck and engulfed in an explosion. However, the command did not provide further details about the intelligence used to establish the vessel's alleged involvement in drug trafficking.The Trump administration has maintained that vessels targeted in such operations since September 2025 were transporting narcotics. US strikes in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific have killed more than 220 people so far.However, the operations have faced mounting criticism from human rights groups and legal experts, who have questioned their legality and described them as extrajudicial killings.Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and independent United Nations experts have called the strikes unlawful extrajudicial killings.Ben Saul, the UN special rapporteur on human rights and counterterrorism, has said there are "reasonable grounds to believe" such attacks "constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law."The American Civil Liberties Union has also criticised the Trump administration's claims against those targeted, calling them "unsubstantiated, fear-mongering claims."You use AI every day. articles.summary: Nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals repatriated from Malaysia arrived in the country’s largest city, Yangon, on Sunday, despite warnings from the United
articles.body: Nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals repatriated from Malaysia arrived in the country’s largest city, Yangon, on Sunday, despite warnings from the United Nations refugee agency and rights groups that conditions for their return remain unsafe.The returnees, including 86 women, had been convicted of illegal stay and other immigration violations in Malaysia, according to Myanmar state media reports.They were transported from Malaysia aboard two navy warships and a hospital ship last Tuesday and arrived in southern Yangon early Sunday, regional government minister Nay Lin Tun said.The group is part of around 5,000 Myanmar nationals who are expected to be repatriated from Malaysia in stages. Malaysia’s home ministry said another 10,388 Myanmar nationals were being held at immigration detention centres.UN, rights groups raise concernsThe repatriation has drawn criticism from the UN high commissioner for refugees and rights groups, who have warned that Myanmar’s security and humanitarian situation remains volatile.They have raised concerns that some returnees could face persecution or forced military conscription in areas affected by the ongoing conflict, the Associated Press reported.“Under international law, the Government of Malaysia is obligated to uphold the principle of non-refoulement and prevent the return of individuals to situations where they face a real risk of persecution, torture, or other serious human rights violations,” Kelley E. Currie, the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, said in a statement on Thursday. “In my assessment, the risk of refoulement in the present circumstances is substantial.”It was not immediately clear whether any Rohingya were among those repatriated. The minority Muslim community has faced persecution in Myanmar and has been denied citizenship.Myanmar has been in turmoil since the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi on February 1, 2021. The coup triggered widespread protests and armed resistance, plunging large parts of the country into conflict.Malaysia is home to around 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the UNHCR, including about 126,000 Rohingya, making it one of Southeast Asia’s largest refugee-hosting communities.However, Malaysia is not a party to the UN Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants.You use AI every day. articles.body: France is set to partially or completely close up to 500 high schools on Monday as days of student protests over poor education standards have escalated into clashes, vandalism and mass arrests, forcing authorities to raise security concerns.According to the BBC, French education minister Édouard Geffray said on Sunday that lessons would be "totally or partly suspended" at 400 to 500 high schools because security conditions had not been fulfilled.Geffray also said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the protests began and that 78 education staff members had been wounded.The protests, which began last week, have spread from Paris to cities including Toulouse, Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille.Students and other demonstrators are protesting over a shortage of teachers, overcrowded classrooms, deteriorating school buildings and a lack of resources.The unrest has triggered a major police response. French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been affected "one way or another" by violent protests, while Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 1,747 people were arrested on Friday, according to the BBC.What are students demandingAt the heart of the protests are demands for more teachers, including substitute staff, as students complain that teacher shortages are disrupting classes and affecting the quality of education.Reuters has independently identified teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating school infrastructure among the main grievances driving the movement.Students are also calling for more resources for schools and better learning conditions. They have raised concerns over overcrowded classrooms and poorly maintained school buildings, with protesters arguing that inadequate infrastructure is making it harder for students to learn.The demonstrations have since escalated into violent clashes in several cities, with protesters confronting riot police and some schools being damaged or ransacked. Reuters has reported arson, attacks on police and widespread arrests as the unrest has spread across France.The government has responded by promising measures to improve school facilities and ensure classes continue, while Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has also pledged changes to the organisation of school days and greater transparency in the university admissions system.You use AI every day. articles.title: Silicon Valley pioneer helped build HP’s first computer and collected wine for 60 years; 6,814 bottles from his cellar went to Christie’s auction
articles.summary: An original Silicon Valley pioneer who helped build Hewlett-Packard's first computer in the 1960s later became a venture capitalist and a key player in
articles.body: An original Silicon Valley pioneer who helped build Hewlett-Packard's first computer in the 1960s later became a venture capitalist and a key player in the modern renaissance of Napa Valley, according to Christie's. His private cellar grew to perhaps as many as 20,000 bottles, and after he died in 2025, Christie's was asked to sell the remaining 6,814 bottles. The sale took place on 5 June 2026 at Rockefeller Centre in New York. Chris Munro, Vice President of Christie’s Wines and Spirits, says every bottle has only ever had one owner and never left the cellar.Silicon Valley trailblazer who helped build Hewlett-Packard's first computer and began a wine cellarAfter graduating from Princeton with an electrical engineering degree, the future collector drove from New Jersey to California in 1964, as the electronics and defence industries were turning Santa Clara Valley into a technology hub. Christie's reports that he took a job at Hewlett-Packard's Palo Alto headquarters, where he helped build the company's first computer.Around the same time, he bought a modest house in the rural town of Woodside, which decades later would be home to leaders of Apple, Sony, Intel and Oracle. Its cool basement soon began filling with wine. He went on to file multiple technology patents, co-found several start-ups and shape digital innovation as a venture capitalist.Napa Valley renaissance: weekend visits to Ridge Vineyard and Joe Heitz when few Americans collectedAt weekends he made the hour-long drive to the newly established Ridge Vineyard, or to see his friend Joe Heitz, the pioneering vintner who was helping usher in Napa's modern era. He came home each time with cases of the latest vintages.Munro told Christie's that at the end of the 1960s very few people in the United States drank fine wine, let alone collected it, because the national taste ran to bourbon and martinis. Napa began to take off around 1968, and this collector was there at the very start.Early client of Kermit Lynch buying Bordeaux and grand cru Burgundy by caseload before prices soaredAs his tastes widened, he became one of the earliest clients of the merchant Kermit Lynch, who opened his shop in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1972. He bought Bordeaux and Burgundy prolifically, at a time when great wines cost far less.Christie’s explains that a case of First Growth Bordeaux may now be worth ten times its 1970s price, and Burgundy has risen even more. The collector bought grand cru wines from producers such as Domaine Armand Rousseau and Domaine Dujac by the case, sometimes for as little as 50 dollars a bottle. Some now change hands for thousands. Collecting then did not require great wealth.Rare Heitz Martha's Vineyard, Ridge Monte Bello 1974, Burgundy and Barolo standouts from the cellarThe sale included twenty vintages of Heitz Cellar Martha's Vineyard going back to 1973, which he had never seen in such quantity. It also offered an eleven-bottle case of Ridge Vineyard Monte Bello from 1974, estimated at 22,000 to 32,000 dollars. Other early Californian names included Inglenook from 1964 to 1968, Mayacamas from 1974, Stag's Leap from 1973 and Freemark Abbey from 1969.Beyond California, Christie's lists Bordeaux from the celebrated 1966 vintage, Petrus and Château Lafleur from the 1960s and 1970s, and Burgundy from Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, Meo-Camuzet and Domaine Georges Roumier. There was also a full unopened case of Gentaz-Dervieux Côte-Rôtie from 1989, eight bottles of Giuseppe Rinaldi Barolo from 1985 and a full case of Bruno Giacosa Barolo from 1967. The sale closed with rare whiskey, including a Van Winkle Special Reserve nineteen-year-old bourbon bottled for Corti Brothers, estimated at 15,000 to 20,000 dollars.Single-owner provenance, impeccable storage and why this cellar was ahead of the curve for collectorsThe cellar is a single-owner collection in the truest sense. The bottles were stored lying down on simple, practical racks, and the team found cases untouched since the 1970s. When space ran out, the collector converted a bathroom into extra storage.A classic, old-school collector who bought what he loved and shared it with friends and family, never for money or investment. He ran his cellar "with curiosity and intellect." He also left behind a large pile of labels, each removed from its case, laminated and filed. The collection was far ahead of its time; a list of the great wines wanted for a modern cellar would look much like this one.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Israel has honoured an intelligence officer who warned of an impending Hamas invasion before the October 7, 2023 attack, three years after the deadly
articles.body: Israel has honoured an intelligence officer who warned of an impending Hamas invasion before the October 7, 2023 attack, three years after the deadly assault exposed major failures in the country’s military and intelligence apparatus.According to a report by The Times of Israel, IDF Chief of Staff Lt Gen Eyal Zamir honoured the Unit 8200 intelligence officer, identified only as Chief Warrant Officer “Vav”, during a conference at the Glilot military base examining the lessons of the October 7 disaster.The officer had warned senior commanders before the attack that Hamas was preparing to invade Israel, but her concerns were not acted upon.The officer, a member of the IDF’s elite Unit 8200 intelligence branch, had raised concerns about Hamas’s preparations for a large-scale assault in the months before October 7.According to The Times of Israel, she sent an email to several officers warning that “the sword is coming” and urged them to take the threat seriously.Her warning came after a September 19, 2023 Unit 8200 dossier that reportedly assessed that Hamas was training for a large-scale invasion of Israel. Despite the intelligence, the assessment did not lead to preparations that could have prevented or mitigated the attack.Zamir said the IDF must ensure that critical voices are heard and that commanders do not suppress warnings that challenge prevailing assessments.“In our organizational culture, we must not allow a culture of pleasing, intellectual tyranny, or suppression of critical thinking,” he said.What happened on October 7The October 7, 2023 attack began when Hamas-led militants launched a coordinated assault from the Gaza Strip into southern Israel. Fighters breached the heavily fortified Gaza border, attacked Israeli military positions and communities, and took hostages back into Gaza.According to Israeli figures, around 1,200 people were killed in the attack, most of them civilians, while around 250 people were taken hostage. The assault became the deadliest attack in Israel’s history and marked the beginning of the ongoing Israel-Hamas war.Israel responded by launching a large-scale military campaign in the Gaza Strip with the stated objective of dismantling Hamas and securing the release of the hostages. The ensuing war has resulted in extensive destruction and a major humanitarian crisis in Gaza.The attack also triggered intense scrutiny of Israel’s military and intelligence establishment, particularly over how Hamas was able to breach the border and carry out such a large-scale assault despite Israel’s extensive intelligence and surveillance capabilities.You use AI every day. articles.summary: US President Donald Trump on Monday confused India with Brazil, claiming that 125 million people had voted in an Indian “presidential election”, while
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Monday confused India with Brazil, claiming that 125 million people had voted in an Indian “presidential election”, while also questioning the integrity of the American voting system.In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote, “125 Million People voted today in the first round of India’s Presidential Election. The results came out shortly after the vote closed, on the same day!”He then compared the alleged election results with the US electoral process, writing, “In Detroit, Philadelphia, California, and numerous other US Cities and States, the results, with much smaller numbers, will often take weeks to Rig, I mean, calculate. Voting in America is corrupt!!!”However, India did not hold a presidential election on Sunday. The President of India is elected indirectly by an electoral college and not through a direct nationwide popular vote.Trump's remarks came after Brazil held the first round of its presidential election on Sunday, with incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro advancing to the October 25 runoff.With 99.99% of the votes counted, Bolsonaro secured 47.03% of the valid votes, while Lula received 45.16%, according to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court.The figure of around 125 million mentioned by Trump is close to Brazil's total valid votes, which stood at about 125.27 million, suggesting he may have confused the Brazilian election with India.Neither Bolsonaro nor Lula crossed the 50% threshold required to win in the first round, triggering the October 25 runoff, BBC reported.Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, outperformed expectations in the first round and finished ahead of Lula. His strong showing has raised the prospect of a shift to the right in Latin America's largest economy.Brazil has used electronic voting for decades, and electoral authorities said the first-round voting process proceeded smoothly.The Organization of American States' electoral observation mission said “the voting has been going smoothly and under adequate safety conditions.”The rapid announcement of results has also been cited as a strength of Brazil's electronic voting system.“When results take a lot of time, it creates an opening for people to cast doubt on the results, to say there’s been a problem,” Josemar Lauriano Pereira, a 46-year-old lawyer in Rio de Janeiro, told the Associated Press.Trump's post drew reactions on social media, with users pointing out that India does not elect its president through a direct popular vote.One user posted, “Trump living in a different world? Is a presidential election taking place in India? President Donald Trump made the incorrect claim that 125 million people voted in India's "presidential election" today.”Another said, “What is my blud Donald Trump smoking? Why is he mentioning India instead of Brazil when talking about the election?”Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: IAF seeks to use a multi-pronged approach to arrest falling fighter strength
articles.summary: The Indian Air Force (IAF) chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh delivered a blunt assessment of the fighter shortage plaguing his organisation.
articles.body: The Indian Air Force (IAF) chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh delivered a blunt assessment of the fighter shortage plaguing his organisation. The reduction in numbers has been eroding the effectiveness of the force for years and shows no sign of easing soon. Speaking in New Delhi ahead of the 94th Air Force Day, Singh said the IAF's current fighter fleet stands at 29 fighter squadrons against a sanctioned strength of 42.5, and that the force needs to induct 36 to 40 new aircraft annually to meet its current requirements. This totals effectively to the induction of two fighter squadrons every year just to arrest the decline. "There is some extra delay, and there is no doubt that it is going to hurt us," he said, pointing squarely at the slow pace of fighter inductions.A significant portion of this delay traces back to Hindustan Aeronautics Limited's production of the Tejas Mark-1A. The IAF has 180 of these jets on order. HAL has committed to manufacturing as many as 24 of these aircraft on an annual basis from here production lines Two of these lines are located in Bengaluru and the other one is located in Nashik.The air force is taking a pragmatic route when it comes to inducting a fifth-generation fighter aircraft. The air force may consider procuring this generation of combat aircraft from abroad only if the domestic programme, the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), faces further delays. Russia has been aggressively pitching the Su-57 fifth generation aircraft to India. Defence Secretary had also recently stated that AMCA remained India's sole path to stealth capability. The induction of this latest generation of operational fighters is important as the China's fleet of these fighters continues to grow and Pakistan is expected to induct a Chinese fighter of this generation. China is also working to operationalise two different types of even more advanced sixth-generation fighter aircraft.On the more immediate procurement front, the Air Force gave the clearest timeline yet for the long-pending 114-aircraft Multi-Role Fighter Aircraft deal, saying it hopes the contract will be signed within the current financial year, which runs through March 2027. The Dassault Rafale remains the clear front-runner, with the bulk of the aircraft expected to be manufactured in India under a Make in India arrangement, building on the existing fleet of 36 Rafales already in service. A portion of this fleet also experienced combat during the active phase of Operation Sindoor last year.The briefing also addressed the Air Force's approach to drones, pushing back on the idea that it needs a separate command structure for unmanned systems, as has been proposed elsewhere, arguing that the force has operated drones for years and sees them as complementary to manned aircraft rather than a parallel silo requiring separate institutional structures. The IAF had in 2022, launched a weapons systems branch that will be designed to handle surface-to-surface missiles, surface-to-air missiles, remotely piloted aircraft and weapon system operators in twin and multi-crew aircraft.The IAF has painted a picture of an air force managing a genuine capability gap through multiple parallel tracks, seeking an expedited Tejas production, pulling private industry into fighter manufacturing, pushing the Rafale deal toward a close and keeping a foreign fifth-generation option in reserve. The air force is clear that capability will come through he indigenous route.
